title: Tindy architecture overview
content:
Tindy helps users find projects and teammates, manage profiles, apply to projects and communicate with other members. This workshop deploys its AWS frontend, backend, database and PDF scanning infrastructure through six CloudFormation templates.
Objectives Deploy stacks in dependency order, use stack Outputs as subsequent inputs, provision a Fresh database, run bootstrap/migration/seed tasks and verify the application through CloudFront. Seeded data supports the login, project discovery, application and review demonstration.
System architecture The diagram shows the arrangement of service groups and application components.
Component Role CloudFront and frontend S3 Deliver the frontend over HTTPS using Origin Access Control for bucket access. CloudFront VPC Origin and internal ALB Route backend requests from CloudFront to the ECS API. ECS Fargate Run the API and one-off database preparation tasks. RDS PostgreSQL Store application data in private DB subnets with TLS connections. Media S3 Store uploads under application prefixes. GuardDuty, EventBridge and SQS Scan PDFs and deliver results to the API worker, with a DLQ for failed processing. Secrets Manager and SSM Store application secrets and Data Protection keys. ECR and GitHub OIDC Store backend images and support GitHub Actions authentication to AWS. CloudWatch and SNS Provide logs, alarms and email notifications. CloudFormation templates Template Scope foundation.yaml S3, ECR, secrets, OIDC and conditional deployment/operations roles. network.yaml VPC, subnets, routes and security groups. database.yaml RDS instance, subnet group and parameter group. integrations.yaml GuardDuty plan, EventBridge rule, SQS/DLQ, SNS and alarms. edge.yaml CloudFront, Origin Access Control, frontend bucket policy and maintenance routing. runtime.yaml ECS, internal ALB, VPC Origin, IAM roles and task definitions. Practical deployment sequence Clean up the existing environment, documented in section 5.7. Import retained Foundation resources, restore the main template and create Network in section 5.3. Create the Fresh Database and Integrations in section 5.4. Create Edge maintenance to obtain its hostname, provision Runtime with DesiredCount 0, prepare and seed the database, enable the API and switch Edge live in section 5.5. Verify and demonstrate the application in section 5.6. This session uses the existing account in us-east-1, a new CloudFront hostname and newly seeded demo data. Deployment pages record verified results and screenshots as execution proceeds.

title: Blog 1
content:
Kiro Workflows: hand off an issue, get back a reviewed PR on staging Original author Poobalan P Source AWS Builder Center Published Nov 17, 2026 Last modified Nov 17, 2026 1. The Task and the Result Poobalan P describes a workflow that takes a GitHub issue, implements the change, runs two independent reviews, and deploys to staging after the operator approves. The author tested it on an issue to add pagination to a sample notes API. After 51 minutes, the run had produced a draft pull request with tests and two review results. CI passed, and the change reached staging. Merging the PR and releasing to production remain decisions for the development team.
Every issue has different requirements. The path through planning, implementation, testing, review, and staging often stays the same. A recipe captures those steps so the next issue follows the same process. The operator supplies the task and the project’s staging instructions for each run.
2. When to Use Chat or a Workflow Topic Ordinary chat Kiro Workflows Planning Discuss and agree on a plan for the current task. Define the steps and their order in a recipe for reuse. Review Ask for an additional review when needed. Run the two reviews in separate sessions each time the recipe runs. Model selection Choose the model for the active conversation. Set a model and effort level for individual steps. Progress Follow the work in the conversation. Inspect running, paused, and completed steps in the Workflows panel. An ordinary chat suits a quick discussion or a typo fix. A workflow is useful when a recurring review and verification process justifies starting several steps, such as when a team routinely prepares similar changes for staging.
3. The YAML Recipe and Step Handoffs The recipe takes two inputs. issue identifies the GitHub issue, and deploy describes how the project deploys to staging and checks the result. A step can declare an agent, model, prompt, and artifacts for other steps to read. The example below shows a shortened intake step. The author’s repository contains the complete recipe.
name: issue-to-deploy inputs: issue: string deploy: prompt steps: - type: step id: intake agent: wf-planner modelId: qwen3-coder-next artifacts: brief: .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/issue.md prompt: > Read GitHub issue {{issue}} and save a short implementation brief. Each step runs in its own session. The plan step needs the issue brief from intake. Reviewers need the diff and the criteria they should check. The verify step needs review results and test commands. Explicit artifact names and locations make those handoffs inspectable.
The Nine Steps from Issue to Staging Step Work Output intake Read the issue and identify its requirements. A brief for the change. plan Plan the implementation and identify the project’s build and test commands. A change plan with verification steps. build Implement the change and add relevant tests. A diff and commit ready for review. code-review Check the behavior, scope, and tests against the issue. Implementation findings. security-review Review the change for security risks. Findings to address before release. gate Combine the reviews and approve only when both reviewers agree. A decision to continue or revise. verify Run checks and prepare the pull request description. Test results, a change summary, and findings worth carrying forward. ship Push the branch, open a draft PR, and wait for CI. A draft pull request and its GitHub checks. deploy Wait for approval, deploy to staging, and run a smoke check. Staging results the operator can verify. The Build–Review Loop and Its Stop Condition The two reviewers run in parallel after build. When either requests a revision, the findings return to the builder for the next round. The workflow pauses for the operator after three rounds without approval. Once both reviewers approve, gate writes APPROVED and the run proceeds.
- type: repeat id: build-and-review maxIterations: 3 onMaxIterations: pause stopCondition: fileCheck: path: .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/gate.json jsonPath: verdict value: APPROVED # Full recipe defines the build, parallel reviews, and gate here. The gate file belongs to the active run. If a previous issue left an approval in gate.json, the stop condition could pick it up before the current reviews finish. The author’s plan step resets the state.
send_message severity Outcome success Continue to the next step. warning Pause for a response. The deploy step uses this to request staging approval. error End the run. A CI failure during ship prevents it from reaching the deploy step. 4. What the Sandbox Run Showed The screenshot shows intake, plan, and build complete. Both reviews are in progress in the first loop, with verify, ship, and deploy queued behind them.
Measure reported by the author Sandbox result Total run time 51 minutes Usage About 37.6 credits Code review alone About 37 minutes and 80% of the run’s credits Command approval requests 62 Build–review rounds Both reviewers approved in the first round These figures come from one sandbox run with a particular effort setting. Code review took most of the time. To compare runs, record the effort, wait time, and credit usage of each step. Approval requests also affect how much attention a run needs from the operator.
A reviewer found a missing test but rated it minor, so the workflow continued. The author updated verify to include minor findings in the PR description. The generated summaries also miscounted tests and acceptance criteria. Reviewing the diff, test list, and original issue together exposes gaps that a summary can miss. Sandbox results and lessons from the original article
5. Preparing a Sandbox Run Set up the environment. Use a version of the Kiro IDE with Workflows, a GitHub remote, and an authenticated GitHub CLI. Enable Workflows in Workspace Configuration and open a new chat. Load the recipe. Get issue-to-deploy.workflow.yaml from the author’s repository. Read its prompts, model choices, iteration limit, and deploy step. If you adapt it for another project, check the edited recipe with validate_workflow before running it. Select the repository and issue. For a sandbox, work from your own fork and enable Issues and Actions as needed. Confirm that GitHub CLI targets the fork. Choose an issue with clear acceptance criteria and start from a clean working tree. The issue description becomes part of the prompts, so review the request and intended scope before running it. Supply the inputs. Give the workflow an issue number, the project’s approved staging process, and a check to perform after deployment. The author’s sandbox uses npm run staging as a demonstration step. For a real staging environment, use its deployment command and health endpoint, with access scoped to staging. Review approval requests. Read the action under review. When the run asks to deploy, check the repository, branch, CI state, and review results before making that decision. Example prompt for the sandbox fork:
Run issue-to-deploy for issue 1 in my sandbox fork. Use npm run staging for the staging demonstration. Pause for my approval before that step and record the verification result in the PR description.
6. Verification and Cleanup gh pr view --web gh pr checks cat .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/gate.json npm test These checks cover the draft PR, GitHub CI, the gate verdict, and the local tests. After deployment, run a smoke check tied to the issue. For pagination, this could include requesting the first and next pages and checking an out-of-range parameter. Record a response or test log so someone else can verify the result.
When the sandbox run is finished, identify its draft PR, branch, and output files. Close the test PR and remove its branch if they are no longer needed. Save evidence required for review before clearing run artifacts. For a shared staging deployment, follow the team’s runbook to hand over or restore the environment.
References Poobalan P’s article on AWS Builder Center The issue-to-deploy recipe on GitHub Sandbox repository used for the example Kiro Workflows documentation

content:
Multi-Agent Orchestration and Multi-Tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Original author Leonid Gimelshtein Source AWS Builder Center Published Nov 17, 2026 Last modified Nov 17, 2026 This architecture connects an orchestrator, specialist agents, and Code Interpreter to a retrieval tool behind AgentCore Gateway. Cedar evaluates who can invoke the tool. Metadata filters limit the documents that can be returned to the tenant and permissions of the user who initiated the request.
1. The Multi-Tenant RAG Problem In a retrieval-augmented generation application, the system retrieves relevant document passages before it sends context to the model. When several organizations share the application and document collection, each organization has its own tenant. Two users from different tenants can ask the same question and receive answers grounded in different documents. Users within one tenant can also have different access based on ownership, group sharing, and visibility.
Multi-agent orchestration creates additional points where document content moves. A request may pass through retrieval, two analyses, a calculation, and report generation. At each boundary, the application needs to identify who coordinates the work, who can invoke the retrieval tool, and what context each agent can receive.
2. One Orchestrator Owns the Request Component Responsibility Next.js backend Verify the user session and determine access scope from trusted application data. Orchestrator Retrieve context, delegate tasks, collect results, and assemble the final response. Agent A and Agent B Accept a focused task and relevant document passages, then return structured results. Interpreter agent Invoke AgentCore Code Interpreter when a calculation or data transformation is needed. AgentCore Gateway and Cedar Authenticate the caller and evaluate permission to invoke the knowledge-base tool under the deployed policy. Knowledge-base tool Construct the filtered retrieval request from verified scope. Bedrock Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch Serverless Run retrieval using the vector index in this architecture. Amazon S3 Store source documents and generated artifacts when the workflow persists them. Suppose a user asks for a summary of QA findings and the proportion in each severity category. The orchestrator retrieves context within the user’s authorized scope. It can ask Agent A to summarize findings and Agent B to extract classification criteria. Both tasks can run in parallel. Once they return, the orchestrator can send selected structured data to the interpreter for the calculation and assemble the final response.
Separate Runtimes and Focused Permissions The example can host the orchestrator and specialists in separate AgentCore Runtimes, using the Strands SDK and Claude on Amazon Bedrock. Each runtime can have its own execution role and tool set. Agent A and Agent B receive the retrieved passages from the orchestrator. Direct access to the knowledge base or permission to write reports is granted only where a specialist task requires it.
The interpreter agent decides what calculation or transformation to perform. Code Interpreter executes it in the processing session. The orchestrator can skip this step for tasks that only need text analysis. Intermediate files and results remain within the scope of the original request.
3. The Tool Invocation and Retrieval Boundaries Retrieval path Orchestrator → AgentCore Gateway → Cedar → knowledge-base tool → Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Control Question Result Gateway policy May the authenticated caller invoke this tool for this request? With enforcement enabled, a denied request stops before the tool runs. Metadata filter built by the tool Which documents may this user read in the current tenant? The Knowledge Base receives a query with metadata conditions and returns matching passages. Permission to invoke the tool allows the request to proceed to the document access check. The tool still needs to obtain tenant, user, and document permissions from server-verified data or an authenticated context. Keeping retrieval behind this interface gives the team a defined place to enforce the filter. AgentCore’s ENFORCE mode applies policy decisions, while LOG_ONLY records them for observation. AgentCore policy enforcement modes
4. Identity Follows the Request Cognito authenticates the user. The Next.js backend validates the token used by its session, including signature, issuer, expiry, and applicable token type and client checks. It resolves tenant membership, user ID, and groups from a trusted source. Service identity authorizes runtime calls. IAM can authorize the backend to invoke the runtime and grant each workload the AWS permissions it needs. Runtime permissions and the user’s document access are evaluated at their respective boundaries. The Gateway receives end-user identity. In this JWT-based design, the orchestrator passes the appropriate access token through the authentication channel. Prompts contain the task and authorized context. The server manages tokens and authorization values. The tool builds the filter from trusted scope. Agent-generated query text describes what to find. Server logic verifies the tenant, user ID, and groups that determine what can be returned. Retrieval stops if the trusted scope is missing. If the Gateway policy needs tenantId, inspect the access token actually issued to the Gateway. A tenant attribute in an ID token does not automatically appear in the access token. AWS documents access-token customization through a pre-token generation trigger for supported Cognito configurations. Customizing Amazon Cognito access tokens
5. An Illustrative Cedar Policy Binds the Tenant This policy illustrates a Gateway with a JWT authorizer. It evaluates an OAuth principal, a specific tool action and Gateway, and the match between the input tenant and the verified claim.
permit ( principal is AgentCore::OAuthUser, action == AgentCore::Action::"kb-tool___queryKnowledgeBase", resource == AgentCore::Gateway::"<gateway-arn>" ) when { principal.hasTag("tenantId") && principal.getTag("tenantId") != "" && context.input.tenantId == principal.getTag("tenantId") }; hasTag checks for the claim before getTag reads it. The sample uses context.input.tenantId for the tenant field supplied to the tool. In a deployment, use the Gateway’s action name and ARN, confirm the input schema, and check the claims issued by the application. Principal-scoped policies · Policy in AgentCore
This condition binds one tool call to the caller’s tenant. Trusted application logic still determines ownership, groups, and administrative permissions. Where several policies apply, verify the combined authorization decision and keep the tenant condition mandatory in the retrieval tool.
6. Filter Metadata Before Context Reaches Agents On ingestion, the application assigns tenantId and ownerId from trusted identity. allowedGroups lists the groups permitted to read the document in that tenant. visibility can represent sharing allowed by the application’s policy. Metadata and document permissions need to stay in sync when access changes.
The example below uses tenant-a, user-123, and the qa group. The Knowledge Base can return passages from documents in tenant-a that the user owns or that are shared with the verified group.
{ "andAll": [ { "equals": { "key": "tenantId", "value": "tenant-a" } }, { "orAll": [ { "equals": { "key": "ownerId", "value": "user-123" } }, { "listContains": { "key": "allowedGroups", "value": "qa" } } ] } ] } The outer andAll requires a tenant match and a match in at least one branch of orAll. listContains checks whether the metadata list contains the specified value. A document in another tenant with the same qa group value fails the outer tenant condition. For multiple verified groups, the tool can add one branch per group. If only one access condition applies, include it directly in andAll, because orAll requires at least two entries. The ingestion and retrieval paths need to account for missing required metadata. Bedrock RetrievalFilter · Configuring Knowledge Base queries
Once retrieval finishes, the orchestrator can distribute the returned passages by task. An analyst may need a subset on a particular topic, while the interpreter may only need an extracted table. Each step receives the material required for its part of the request.
7. Tenant Scope After Retrieval Derived data How the application preserves scope Conversation history Resolve a saved or resumed session using the appropriate tenant and identity. Retrieval and response caches Partition by tenant and the relevant access scope. Account for permission changes when refreshing or invalidating entries. Interpreter files Bind sessions and storage locations to the request. Limit inputs to the files needed for the calculation. Reports and exported files Associate results with the tenant and access policy. Check current permission before returning a saved artifact. Logs and traces Record request identifiers and decision points for investigation. Keep access tokens and document contents out of operational logs. The supplied write-up reports two findings for the scenarios it covered. Unauthorized requests were rejected, and retrieval stayed within the user’s permitted scope. The following example checks show which boundary to inspect for each expected result.
Verification case Expected evidence An authorized caller owns a document in the tenant The Gateway permits the tool call. The tool sends a filter and the returned context can include eligible passages. A user belongs to a group with document access The filter uses the verified group and can return matching documents within the tenant. The shared index contains a document from another tenant Its content is absent from retrieval results, specialist context, and reports for the active tenant. The tenant scope is unverified The request stops before retrieval. The application does not run an unfiltered search. A user opens a saved report The application checks the tenant and current read permission before returning the artifact. 8. Putting the Architecture Together Cognito and Next.js establish end-user identity. An orchestrator coordinates AgentCore Runtimes where the Strands SDK defines agent behavior and Claude on Bedrock performs analysis. Gateway and Cedar control access to the knowledge-base tool, which supplies mandatory tenant filtering for Bedrock Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch Serverless. Amazon S3 holds source documents and retained artifacts. Code Interpreter handles computation when needed. AWS CDK describes the infrastructure for repeatable deployments.
When adding a specialist or changing how a report is calculated, the team can trace the request back to its authenticated caller, the policy decision, and the filtered passages supplied to the agents. Those records give the team concrete places to verify access as the workflow evolves.

title: Proposal
content:
Tindy — AI-Powered Project & Teammate Matching Platform on AWS Student Author: Cao Thành Nhân
Role: Frontend Engineer (React / TypeScript / Tailwind CSS) & Backend Optimization (CORS, Rate Limiting)
Project: Tindy — AI-Powered Community & Project Matching Platform
Target Community: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Community
1. Executive Summary Tindy is an AI-powered web platform designed specifically for the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) student community, bridging the gap between individuals seeking project opportunities and teams looking for specific technical competencies.
In student tech communities, recruitment and team-formation details are frequently scattered across unstructured channels such as Facebook groups, Discord servers, and direct messages. Introverted students often hesitate to initiate conversations with strangers, while project leaders struggle to locate candidates with the exact skills required (for instance, a team having solid frontend and backend developers but lacking an AI/ML engineer). Tindy resolves this challenge through an intelligent, transparent matching mechanism:
For Students/Members: Build a centralized technical profile; explore recommended projects with transparent Match Scores; express interest via intuitive actions (Interested, Skip, Save for Later); understand recommendations via AI Explain Match; and chat directly with project leads within the platform. For Project Leaders: Post project opportunities with structured requirements akin to Job Descriptions; receive curated candidate recommendations; manage applications and send invitations; and track open positions and team seats in real time. The system is architected as a Cloud-Native solution on AWS (US East, us-east-1). The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, bundled using Vite, and served globally via Amazon CloudFront backed by private Amazon S3 storage with Origin Access Control (OAC). The backend uses ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) deployed on containerized Amazon ECS Fargate behind an Internal Application Load Balancer (ALB) routed through CloudFront VPC Origins. The solution is powered by Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 17, Amazon Bedrock for generative AI features, and AWS GuardDuty, EventBridge, and SQS for secure asynchronous file processing.
2. Problem Statement, Solution, and Functional Scope 2.1. Problem Statement Hesitation in Cold Outreach: Introverted students often feel uncomfortable messaging strangers directly (“Can I join your project?”), missing out on valuable collaborative opportunities despite having matching skills. Missing Complementary Skillsets: Project teams frequently form around existing circles of friends, resulting in duplicate skillsets while lacking vital specialized roles (e.g., Cloud/DevOps or AI engineering). Fragmented Professional Profiles: Evidence of student competence is dispersed across GitHub, LinkedIn, AWS certification badges, and static CV files, making qualification verification tedious for team leads. Disjointed Communication: Fragmented communication across third-party chat apps leads to lost recruitment context and uncoordinated team finalization. Limitations of Keyword Matching: Traditional keyword filtering fails to recognize semantic alignment between project requirements (“Experience with RAG systems and LLMs”) and student descriptions (“Built an AI chatbot using Amazon Bedrock and pgvector”). 2.2. Proposed Solution Tindy establishes a streamlined, end-to-end recruitment lifecycle:
Student Profile + Project Requirements (JD) ↓ AI Matching Engine (Deterministic Rules + Semantic Similarity) ↓ Recommended Projects ↓ Student clicks "Interested" ↓ Project Lead reviews candidate profile & AI explanation ↓ Internal Real-Time Chat (SignalR WebSocket) ↓ Acceptance & Team Membership (Seat count updated) Unlike traditional dating applications, Tindy does not feature user-to-user swiping. Instead, students interact directly with Projects and Positions. This approach preserves professional dignity, minimizes fear of rejection, and fosters a collaborative community ethos.
2.3. Functional Scope Workflow Frontend Action (UI) Backend & System Processing Profile Building & AI Extraction Member enters technical skills, preferred roles, and availability (hrs/week). Can upload CV PDF or text for Amazon Bedrock extraction. UI displays a structured draft of skills and experience. Member reviews, edits, and saves the verified data to PostgreSQL. Project Discovery & Application Member browses recommended projects, views Match Scores, and selects Interested, Skip, or Save. Application status is marked as Pending. Project lead receives notification of a new interested candidate. Candidate Management & Approval Lead reviews candidate list by position, inspects profile details and AI match reasons, then clicks Accept or Decline. On acceptance, API verifies eligibility and seat availability; candidate becomes a project member; position seat count increments. Internal Real-Time Chat Members and leaders communicate 1-on-1 or within project workspace chat rooms. Messages are delivered instantly over WebSockets via SignalR. Backend Rate Limiting prevents spamming and flooding. Release & Operations Engineers build and deploy static frontend to S3, build Docker images to ECR, and orchestrate CloudFormation stacks. The entire platform operates under a unified HTTPS CloudFront hostname with maintenance mode and /api/health/ready verification. 2.4. Match Scoring Formula and AI Explain Match Match scores are calculated using a deterministic weighted formula combined with semantic analysis, ensuring objective and predictable recommendations:
$$\text{Match Score} = (0.40 \times S_{\text{required}}) + (0.30 \times S_{\text{role}}) + (0.20 \times S_{\text{availability}}) + (0.10 \times S_{\text{optional}})$$
Required Technical Skills (40%): Proportion of mandatory skills possessed by the student. Preferred Role (30%): Alignment between the student’s career focus (e.g., Frontend Developer) and the open position. Availability (20%): Comparison between student’s available hours/week and project commitment requirements. Optional / Bonus Skills (10%): Nice-to-have technical skills. Frontend AI Explain Match Card: The user interface does not merely display a percentage (e.g., 88% Match); it provides an interactive popover detailing:
Strong Matches: Proficient in React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS; Matches Frontend Role; Meets 10 hrs/week commitment. Skill Gap: No prior experience noted with Next.js or GraphQL (offering targeted guidance for future learning). 3. Solution Architecture 3.1. Layered Architecture Frontend Layer: Engineered with React 18 and TypeScript, bundled with Vite for fast load times and clean modular code. Modern, responsive styling implemented with Tailwind CSS. Client state and server data caching managed through React Context / Custom Hooks and typed HTTP clients. Real-time bidirectional communication powered by @microsoft/signalr. Stored in a private Amazon S3 bucket and distributed globally through Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC). Edge & Routing Layer: Amazon CloudFront acts as the single reverse proxy: Static assets (/*): Cached at edge locations from the S3 bucket. Dynamic API routes (/api/*): Forwarded through CloudFront VPC Origins to the internal ALB with caching disabled. Real-time Chat routes (/hubs/*): Supports WebSocket connection upgrade (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols) to backend tasks. Application & Backend Layer: ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) following Clean Architecture (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, API). Packaged as a Docker container stored in Amazon ECR, executed serverlessly on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate within private subnets. Data & Storage Layer: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 17 deployed in private database subnets with TLS encryption. Amazon S3 Media Bucket (Private) for avatar images and CV documents. AWS GuardDuty Malware Protection scans uploaded PDFs $\rightarrow$ EventBridge captures scan verdicts $\rightarrow$ Amazon SQS queues asynchronous processing $\rightarrow$ updates file validity before AI processing. AI Layer: Integrates Amazon Bedrock for CV parsing, automated profile summarization, and match explanations. 3.2. Author’s Technical Contributions (Frontend & Backend) As the Frontend Engineer and Backend Contributor on project Tindy, Cao Thành Nhân personally led the implementation of:
Frontend Responsibilities: Client Architecture: Designed the modular component structure, enforced strict typing with TypeScript, and established the UI design system using Tailwind CSS. Core User Interfaces: Authentication & Onboarding: Interactive login/register views and profile initialization wizards. Interactive Profile Builder: Skill tag selectors, availability commitment sliders, CV preview, and the AI Profile Draft Review component. Project Discovery & Matching: Project recommendation cards, match percentage badges, Explain Match popovers, and quick interaction buttons (Interested, Skip, Save). Team Management & Candidate Review: Project Lead management table, interested candidate review modal, and acceptance/rejection workflows. Real-Time Chat Interface: Embedded messaging component with typing indicators, real-time message streams, and active connection management. Network & WebSocket Integration: Integrated @microsoft/signalr with automatic reconnection; normalized API calls through the unified CloudFront origin (/api). Backend Contributions & Optimizations: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Configuration: Fine-tuned and secured CORS policies in ASP.NET Core (Program.cs), permitting authorized CloudFront distribution domains and local development environments to communicate seamlessly with /api/* and WebSocket endpoints without browser security blocks. Message Request Throttling & Rate Limiting: Implemented rate-limiting middleware for chat message submission and SignalR hubs. Mitigated spamming and flood requests that could degrade ECS Fargate container performance or incur runaway cloud costs. Ensured messaging stability and high availability during concurrent student interactions. 4. Implementation and Testing 4.1. Six CloudFormation Stacks Infrastructure is codified using 6 decoupled AWS CloudFormation templates:
Order Stack Name Template Key Resources 1 tindy-foundation foundation.yaml S3 Buckets, ECR Repository, Secrets Manager, IAM Roles, GitHub OIDC Provider. 2 tindy-network network.yaml VPC (2 AZs), Public/Private Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateway, Security Groups. 3 tindy-database database.yaml RDS PostgreSQL 17 (db.t4g.micro), DB Subnet Group, Parameter Group. 4 tindy-integrations integrations.yaml GuardDuty Malware Plan, EventBridge Rule, SQS Queue, DLQ, CloudWatch Alarms. 5 tindy-runtime runtime.yaml ECS Cluster, Fargate Task Definition, Internal ALB, CloudFront VPC Origin. 6 tindy-edge edge.yaml CloudFront Distribution, Origin Access Control (OAC), Cache Behaviors, Maintenance Routing. 4.2. CI/CD & Frontend Deployment Workflow Backend Deployment: GitHub Actions builds ASP.NET Core Docker images, pushes them to ECR with pinned digests, and updates the ECS task definition with zero-downtime rolling deployment. Frontend Deployment: Build execution: npm run build generates the production-optimized dist/ bundle. Synchronization: GitHub Actions (assuming FrontendDeployRole via secure OIDC) synchronizes assets to the S3 bucket using aws s3 sync. Edge Invalidation: Executes aws cloudfront create-invalidation --paths "/*" to purge edge caches immediately. Maintenance Mode: The Edge template supports dynamic switching between maintenance (serving a static maintenance page from S3) and live (routing dynamic requests to ALB). 5. Timeline and Sprint Plan The implementation spans 7 weeks (Weeks 4 to 10 of the internship curriculum):
Sprint Timeline Frontend & Backend Development Focus Deliverables Sprint 1 Weeks 4–5 • UI/UX wireframing.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS Emulator: First Impressions From a Real Serverless App Original author Ran Isenberg Source Ran The Builder Published Nov 12, 2026 Last modified Nov 13, 2026 Ran Isenberg experimented with moving integration tests for the AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook from deployed AWS resources to AWS Emulator. The first full run reported 34 passing integration tests in about seven seconds. The Lambda application code and individual test bodies stayed the same. The main changes involved starting the test environment, setting the SDK endpoint, and adapting the test setup around behavior the tested emulator build handled differently. Original article and experiment results
1. The Serverless Testing Pyramid Before the Change The previous workflow used an ephemeral stack, a temporary deployment in an AWS test account that could be created for a branch. Unit tests and infrastructure definition checks ran locally. Developers could launch integration tests from their IDE, but those tests still called services from the deployed stack. End-to-end tests exercised the deployed application along the path a client would use.
This approach gives developers feedback from the AWS services themselves. It also adds a deployment or update before branch-level integration testing. Giving an AI coding agent the ability to run those tests raises a second question about where deployment credentials should live. The author’s goal was to keep the edit-and-test loop local while leaving access to the AWS account in a controlled delivery pipeline.
Mocks already had a place in the old workflow. They helped make a particular dependency fail on demand so a test could check the application’s response. Isenberg also describes using Moto for a case that needed a simulated organization with 10,000 accounts. Different tools are useful depending on what a particular test needs to prove. The author’s testing approach
2. Where AWS Emulator Sits in the Test Process AWS Emulator exposes a local endpoint that implements AWS APIs for development and testing. AWS documents native Linux packages and a Docker path for Windows, macOS, and other supported setups. In this example, pytest still runs the handler in its own process. The SDK uses AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to route the relevant requests to the emulator, which maintains resource state for the run. AWS Emulator User Guide
Call the handler with a test event. The handler executes the application logic and data-access layer used by the service. Return mocked results inside the test process. A fixture can supply an AppConfig feature flag or another deliberately fixed dependency response. Send SDK requests to the local endpoint. The diagram uses https://127.0.0.1:9297. A DynamoDB write and a later read can use the same emulated table. Check the response and the stored state. An order creation case can inspect the handler’s response and read back the order. A repeated-request case can check that the application handles the same request without creating an unexpected second order. The local test job uses emulator credentials when request signing is required and configures its SDK to trust the emulator’s CA. Real AWS credentials stay outside the job. The setup checks the effective endpoint before running tests and stops on a missing or unexpected configuration. This is especially useful when an SDK client has its own endpoint settings. Pointing an AWS SDK at AWS Emulator
3. Moving Integration Tests Before Deployment Test layer Where it runs in the revised setup What it covers Unit Local or CI Business rules, input validation, and logic isolated from services. Infrastructure Local or CI before deployment Expectations about declared resources and values in the infrastructure definition. Integration Local or CI with the emulator and selective mocks The handler, SDK, and emulated resources working together within the test’s scope. End-to-end A test stack on AWS API Gateway reaching Lambda, real identity integration, IAM roles and policies, and deployed configuration. A developer or coding agent can update code, run unit and integration tests, and open a pull request from an environment without AWS account access. CI repeats linting, type checks, unit tests, and emulator integration tests. After approval, the deployment job uses scoped AWS permissions to create the test stack, run end-to-end checks, and remove temporary resources from that run.
The CI/CD permissions establish this separation. Pointing an SDK at loopback changes where its configured requests go. The integration job’s identity still determines whether it could reach real AWS through another path. AWS also documents that IAM and resource policy evaluation in the emulator differs from AWS. IAM and deployed security checks therefore belong on a controlled AWS test stack. AWS Emulator limitations
4. What the AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook Experiment Covered The sample Python service lets a client sign in and call API Gateway to create, retrieve, list, or delete orders. Lambda validates requests and runs the business logic. One DynamoDB table stores orders. The other supports idempotency through Powertools. Cognito issues user tokens, AppConfig supplies runtime feature flags, and AWS CDK defines the deployed stack. AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook
The migration added a Makefile path for starting the emulator locally and made the emulator a CI dependency. The integration job moved before deployment and checked its endpoint to avoid using a live AWS account. The first full run passed 34 integration tests in roughly seven seconds. This is a measurement of the author’s suite and environment. In a different project, measure emulator startup, test data preparation, and test execution separately when making a comparison. Original article · Migration pull request
Component Treatment in the reported experiment What the result covers DynamoDB The handler uses the SDK to call the emulated tables. Order persistence and the Powertools idempotency store exercised by the suite. Lambda and API Gateway pytest builds sample events and invokes Python handlers directly. Handler logic and its dependencies. The deployed API Gateway-to-Lambda path belongs to E2E. AppConfig The existing mock stays in the suite. Application behavior for feature-flag values provided by the fixtures. Cognito The local suite uses test-only tokens suited to its application scenarios. The local authentication path exercised by the fixtures. Live signing-key retrieval and user pool behavior remain checks for AWS E2E. The distinction matters when interpreting the reported result. The local suite exercised the handlers, order data, and idempotency together. It did not exercise the emulator’s own Lambda or API Gateway implementation. The deployed suite verifies the wiring that sits outside the in-process test.
5. Four Approaches When an API Behaves Differently Approach When it helps What the team takes on Deploy a test stack to AWS The test depends on live IAM, deployed configuration, or cross-service behavior. Deployment time, resource cost, and management of test account access. Mock calls in-process The test needs a deliberate failure or needs to isolate application logic. Mock responses need maintenance when service contracts or assumptions change. Use the emulator with small workarounds Most required APIs behave as expected and the remaining gaps can be isolated with fixtures. Document the behavior each workaround leaves to E2E and recheck it after upgrades. Combine the emulator with another container An external dependency needs an engine’s behavior, such as PostgreSQL for migrations or ORM queries. Run another service on the test machine or runner. An engine container covers database behavior within its setup, while deployed RDS configuration still needs its own checks. In the build Isenberg tested, emulated Cognito issued ES256-signed tokens while the live Cognito flow used by the suite expected RS256. The reported user pool scenario also did not invoke Lambda triggers. A local token fixture kept the application scenarios runnable and left the live Cognito behavior to end-to-end tests. Isenberg discusses using a real PostgreSQL engine in a separate container as an option for relational workloads. The Cookbook uses DynamoDB, so the PostgreSQL approach was outside the reported experiment. Trade-offs in the original article
When a difference appears, start with the purpose of the test. A failure fixture may be enough when the question is how the application reacts. When the question is whether an AWS service actually behaves that way, record which AWS check provides the evidence. That makes the cost of each workaround visible when the test suite changes.
6. Reading Compatibility Evidence by Release The author recorded 6,908 reports in the known-gaps directory on November 12, 2026. This number describes the repository at the time of the review. For a project decision, check whether the specific operations and failure cases your application uses are covered. A broad service label or score can hide differences between managing a resource and using its data plane. The author’s observations
Amazon describes three groups of agents behind the original project. One group develops reference tests using AWS. Another identifies differences in the emulator. The third fixes those differences and submits changes through automated checks. Isenberg raised a question about public visibility of the tests. AWS documentation now points to the public AWS Emulator Evaluation Suite and explains how fidelity scores relate to releases. Compare scores against the same version of the evaluation suite when judging changes. How Amazon built AWS Emulator · AWS guidance on fidelity · Evaluation Suite repository
7. Evaluating the Emulator for Another Repository Inventory the AWS calls. Read the application code, CDK or Terraform configuration, and existing tests. Identify the data-plane calls and deployment behavior each test depends on. Try a small representative path. Run one integration case from the handler through the SDK to an emulated resource. Record the emulator version, endpoint, fixtures, and observed behavior. Use sample data and emulator-only credentials. Record the coverage boundary. For each mock or workaround, state what the local test covers and which AWS test verifies the remaining behavior. Keep a controlled E2E path from the client to deployed services. Revisit the result after updates. Run the same tests against a new emulator version and compare against the expected AWS contract. Remove a workaround once the relevant project scenario passes with the standard path. The author packaged this evaluation into an AWS Emulator adoption skill. It inventories application and infrastructure dependencies, checks relevant operations locally, and produces a report of compatibility and workarounds. The Cookbook’s emulator configuration is a second reference for teams planning a similar trial. AWS Emulator adoption skill · Cookbook emulator configuration
For the Cookbook, the emulator made the integration loop faster because the core tests exercised application code against sufficiently compatible DynamoDB operations. A useful test record names the layers each result actually covered. Local checks surface application issues early, and the deployed suite verifies the configuration and access controls the application will use on AWS.
